questions.stem: A staging table can hold several versions of the same OrderID. You need the latest version of each order, by IngestedAt. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY OrderID ORDER BY IngestedAt DESC) and keep row 1
Keep only the rows whose IngestedAt equals the overall maximum IngestedAt value in the staging table
SELECT DISTINCT * FROM staging so that repeated versions of each OrderID collapse into one
GROUP BY OrderID and take MAX of every column, so each order keeps its newest values

questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the key and ordered by recency picks exactly one, newest, row per order. DISTINCT removes only rows identical in every column, MAX of each column can mix values from different versions, and the overall maximum keeps only the last batch.

questions.stem: At Larkspur, orders arrive for customers the Customer dimension doesn't have yet. What should the load do so these orders aren't lost and reports stay correct?

options.text: Load the orders with a NULL customer key and leave that key NULL permanently, even after the customer reaches the Customer dimension later
Stop the pipeline with an error and rerun the whole load from scratch once the CRM sends the missing customer records
Insert an inferred member: a Customer row with the business key and placeholder attributes, and update it when the CRM data arrives
Drop those orders from the load and insert them only once the customer has arrived in the Customer dimension

questions.explanation: An inferred member gives the fact row a real surrogate key now. When the customer's details arrive, the same row is updated, so the facts already loaded need no change.

questions.stem: In PySpark, how do you replace NULL values in the country column with "Unknown"?

options.text: df.where("country = 'Unknown'")
df.replace(None, "country")
df.dropna("country")
df.fillna({"country": "Unknown"})

questions.explanation: fillna (also na.fill) replaces NULLs, and a dictionary limits it to the named columns. dropna removes rows instead.

questions.stem: At Larkspur, a retried run sometimes lands the same batch twice. Which two changes make the silver load safe to repeat? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: MERGE the batch into the silver table on OrderID, updating matches and inserting the rest
Keep appending, and add more retries
Turn off the pipeline's retry setting and accept failed nights
Append, then rely on reports to use DISTINCT
Overwrite only the batch's own slice of the table (for example with replaceWhere on its load date) instead of appending

questions.explanation: A MERGE on the business key and a replace of the batch's own slice both give the same table however often the batch runs. More retries make duplicates more likely, and pushing DISTINCT onto every report leaves the table wrong.

questions.stem: Log records are appended to a Delta table, and the source sometimes resends records that are already in the table. Each record has a uniqueId. Which statement adds only the new records?

options.text: `INSERT INTO logs SELECT * FROM newDedupedLogs`
`INSERT OVERWRITE logs SELECT * FROM newDedupedLogs`
`MERGE INTO logs USING newDedupedLogs ON logs.uniqueId = newDedupedLogs.uniqueId WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *`
`MERGE INTO logs USING newDedupedLogs ON logs.uniqueId = newDedupedLogs.uniqueId WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *`

questions.explanation: An insert-only merge inserts only records whose uniqueId isn't already in the table. A plain insert duplicates resent records, an update-only merge never adds new ones, and an overwrite drops existing data.

questions.stem: A MERGE into a silver Delta table fails because several source rows match the same target row. What should you do?

options.text: Run the same MERGE again, because the second attempt picks one row
Add a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE clause
Change WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE to WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
Deduplicate the source so that only one row per key remains before the merge

questions.explanation: Only one source row can match a given target row; otherwise the update is ambiguous. Preprocess the source to remove the multiple matches.

questions.stem: A stream receives duplicate events with the same guid up to 6 hours apart. Which code removes all duplicates while keeping the state bounded?

options.text: `df.distinct()` with no watermark
`df.withWatermark("eventTime", "10 hours").dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["guid"])`
`df.dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["guid"])` with no watermark
`df.withWatermark("eventTime", "1 hour").dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["guid"])`

questions.explanation: The watermark threshold must be greater than the largest time gap between duplicates (6 hours), and dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark requires a watermark. A 1-hour watermark misses late duplicates, and distinct without a watermark lets state grow indefinitely.

questions.stem: Last week a fact load inserted an inferred member for customer C-881, with Unknown attributes and IsInferredMember set to TRUE. Today the customer's real details arrive. What should the dimension load do?

options.text: Leave the inferred row and insert a second row for the real customer
Expire the inferred row and insert a new SCD type 2 version
Update the attributes on the existing row and set IsInferredMember to FALSE
Delete the inferred row and insert the customer with a new surrogate key

questions.explanation: Changes to an inferred member are treated as late arriving details, not SCD changes: update the attributes in place and clear the flag, so facts keep their key.

questions.stem: A customer DataFrame must drop rows only where both c_acctbal and c_custkey are null, and keep rows where only one of them is null. Which code does this?

options.text: `df.na.fill("0", subset=["c_acctbal", "c_custkey"])`
`df.na.drop()`
`df.na.drop("all", subset=["c_acctbal", "c_custkey"])`
`df.na.drop("any", subset=["c_acctbal", "c_custkey"])`

questions.explanation: na.drop with all drops a row only when all listed columns are null. any drops a row if either is null, no arguments checks every column for any null, and fill replaces nulls instead of dropping rows.

questions.stem: A streaming aggregation uses `withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")`. Which two statements about late-arriving records are true? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: Records later than the threshold are guaranteed to be included in their window
A longer watermark tolerates later data but keeps more state and delays results
Records that arrive within the 10-minute threshold are always processed
Watermarks are optional for stream-stream outer joins
The watermark has no effect on how much state the query keeps

questions.explanation: Records within the threshold are always processed; later ones might be, with no guarantee. Longer watermarks raise late-data tolerance at the cost of state and latency. Watermarks are mandatory for outer joins and they bound state.
